newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: FEATURE - Bangladesh struggles to end flesh trade.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bangladesh struggles to end flesh trade.

text.p: Thirteen-year-old Beauty had to entertain five clients each day during her two months in a Dhaka brothel before she was rescued by a women lawyers' group.

"They came of all ages, had different taste and demands. I had to satisfy them, to the best of my ability, to escape torture," the girl said, two days after she was housed in a shelter run by the Bangladesh National Women Lawyers' Association (BNWLA).
The girl is part of a horrific chain of abuse and murder affecting Bangladeshi women.
"It's hard to believe...but it's the truth. It's the cruel reality we face," said Salma Ali, executive director of the association.
The home, which can accommodate at most 30 girls even if they share beds and sleep on the floor, has been the last hope for some girls.
They have little prospect of being restored to their parents, having a family or living freely.
"My mother has refused to take me back because her second husband would not accept me," said 10-year-old Tiya.
Pinky, 14, was rescued by police and handed over to BNWLA.
"I managed to escape just by sheer luck. A deal was made between the man who stole me from my family and a prospective buyer for 100,000 taka ($2,500)," she said.
"I overheard their conversation. I was to be smuggled to India. I was preparing for a life in brothel or even worse but the BNWLA rescued me," she said.
Also in the BNWLA home was Rahima, who was married in 1993. "I had almost three years of married life but suddenly my husband started to change.
"One day he cut off one of my hands, one leg and a ear. That was not enough for him. He tied me up and left me on a train line where someone found and brought me to this home."
BNWLA trained Rahima to teach knitting to other girls at the shelter.

"This is an unending story of unfolding tragedies," said Salma Ali, a senior lawyer. The girls at the shelter said they loved Ali very much. "She is just mother-like, caring, highly disciplined and a good administrator," Rahima told Reuters.
Ali's work continues outside the shelter.
Juthi, 17, does not live in the home but visits Ali almost every week, along with her sister Moyna.
Juthi was rescued with BNWLA's help while she was being smuggled into India. The BNWLA is helping Moyna in her search for her son, who was picked up by a family friend one day but never seen again.
"We deal with a variety of cases -- trafficking, torture, rape, prostitution," Ali said.
She said she was investigating reports of smuggled women and children not only being sexually abused but also killed for their body parts.
"If only part of the reports we have are true I can say humanity is in danger at a time when everybody talks about human rights," she said.

A draft report prepared by BNWLA member Mominul Islam said confessions made by some traffickers arrested by police revealed that "corneas, kidneys and blood extracted from children" were sold at a high price, especially in India.
It said Bangladeshis smuggled to India were also killed and their skeletons sold.
"India is the world's biggest skeleton exporter. But Indian people are mostly Hindus who are cremated; the Moslems are very sensitive and their bodies cannot be used for skeleton exports.

"Then the likelihood is that most of the skeletons come from people smuggled in from other countries. The traffickers are possibly the main source for supplying kidneys, blood, corneas in the Indian hospitals and clinics," the report said.
A 1995 Bangladeshi law providing for the death sentence as the maximum penalty for torture, rape, trafficking and killing of women and children has also been largely ineffective, lawyers said.
BNWLA said some 200,000 Bangladeshi women were smuggled to Pakistan alone over the last 10 years.
Most victims come from poor families and are lured by traffickers on fake promises of jobs, marriage and good life, Ali said.
"Trying to save the victims and curb the growing flesh trade has been an uphill task. But we will not to give up."
